seg:
toward a theoretical maximum:
formal science in basic education
- a shared hallucination

preface

Who am I to say? I am not an educator, or a mathematician, or a scientist, or an academic of any kind. I am merely an opinionated retiree with time on my hands for watching such inspiring videos as Leonard Susskind's theoretical minimum lecture series. My expertise in any of the subjects I pontificate on below, to put it politely, is of modest depth and considerable fragility. But I will continue as if I know what I am talking about. One might easily describe this effort as an academic exercise in it's least flattering sense. But the exercise is the thing.

The formal and natural sciences are complementary. Here science classifies both, and we refer to a curriculum for a basic scientific education. This page outlines a possible method for determining the topics in formal science and their order of presentation that would be included in the curriculum, and outlines an example method implementation.
We assume basic education has two main (knowledge related) responsibilities. First, provide a minimal level of education expected of all members of society. Second, provide students prerequisites for continuing studies required for future careers. In our case, the future careers are STEM-related, where STEM is an acronym for science, technology, engineering, and mathematics. It is relatively accurate to say on average only 25 percent of students will continue with STEM-related studies and careers. These students require a practitioner's knowledge of science, while 100 percent of students require a non-practitioner's knowledge of science. It is clear that the desiderata for curriculum design should include a complementary integration of these responsibilities.

 It is difficult to talk of the future of education without acknowledging the uncertainty of the role of AI, i.e. machine based intelligence. If such intelligent agency remains benign to indifferent, it is easy to imagine each child soon having a dedicated context used for interfacing with and individualizing educational resources. It is harder to imagine the social context of a basic education, which thankfully is well out of scope. But whatever the future, this context highlights our goal here: present one path among many that might be made available to future students.

It is difficult to describe this page if not a hallucination I share with LLM AI.

introduction

The first step in curriculum design is choosing a goal. Here we choose to maximize a student's knowledge of physical reality. This is by no means a practical choice. Without years of continuing education, this knowledge has no practical use. I have heard arguments that conclude only practical knowledge matters. As I am in no position to confirm or deny such arguments, it must be said that the chosen goal may require significant cognitive effort for no return. Yet we're relaxed; we are only exploring our options. But the exercise should include the requirement that this knowledge is complementary to the practical knowledge related to STEM-related careers.

We can describe the target knowledge in general terms. Specifically, it is not merely conceptual, it is formal.

No one theory describes physical reality. Perhaps the most important and inclusive theory, the standard model of particle physics, is out of reach. Just as well. The dynamics of particle interactions of high energy physics are no doubt fundamental to understanding physical reality, but are quite detached from everyday experience. General relativity is closer at hand; it also depends on a more limited and quite elegant geometric formalization. And it describes gravity, something we experience every day; but it only describes gravity.

We choose to formally describe quantum statistical mechanics.

We have our goal. The second step in curriculum design of formal science is to choose the foundation, where one starts. We choose classical logic and basic set theory as our foundation. The next step is determining the critical path, the one which has a minimal cognitive load, from formalization of foundational concepts to formalization of quantum statistical mechanics.

We describe core topics, non-core topics, and STEM-related topics. A core topic lies on the critical path, while a non-core topic, which still may be of general interest, does not. On the other hand, a STEM-oriented topic is often a requirement for future study. However, these classifications highlight dependency relations; one would hope each student is allowed to follow a path of their choosing. Additionally, there is no clear line to discriminate between topics designed for the general or STEM-oriented student.

Core topics are collected into general subjects areas, which are then presented in the specified order:
  • part I
    • propositional logic
    • formal statements
    • numbers
  • part II
    • Bayesian inference
    • quantum logic
    • quantum Bayesian inference

and we are done, since quantum Bayesian inference and quantum statistical mechanics share the same formal model.

With respect to the relation between the proposed curriculum and current curricula, the impact is proportional to the grade level. We assume a 0-12 grade basic education. Around grade 3-4 propositional logic would be introduced, and around grade 5-6 formal statements would be introduced. Once our formal definitions of numbers is introduced around grade 7-8, one would expect significant modification of topics in mathematics for the general student.

Even before children begin their basic education, they have mastered their native language. This entails recognition of logical (truth) connectives, as well as an understanding of the relationship between propositions and truth values. The role of propositional logic is not to introduce the student to novel concepts, as these have long since been mastered. It is the ground upon which we introduce formal science. And, we have now exposed the student to Boolean logic.

Formal statements implicitly reflect our foundational choices. We adopt the perspective axiomatized by ZF set theory. As the only type is set, we can use the language of classical single-sorted first order predicate logic. This means we want to expose the student to (simple) quantified predicate expressions. As a predicate is a function, and a function is between sets, the subject area introduces these topics as well.

Our definitions of numbers are key to limiting the cognitive load of the core path. Much of standard mathematics is built upon choices of a set's topology and sigma-algebra. These establish spaces one may describe as continuous and/or measurable. Our definitions of numbers provide a framework for nonstandard analysis and measure via discrete but transfinite arithmetic, bypassing continuous mathematics, which now (mostly) becomes a STEM-related topic.

We use nonstandard analysis to formally validate the mathematics of Bayesian Inference. Although we could now model classical statistical mechanics, we don't; rather we continue with our formal topics. We again use nonstandard analysis to validate quantum logic.

Retrofitting quantum for Boolean logic, we formalize quantum Bayesian inference.

We note nonstandard analysis, though helpful for formalizing mathematical concepts, usually falls short with respect to calculational efficiency. This is why continuous mathematics is required for future STEM-related study.

The page includes embedded UIs that prototype some relevant educational tools, mostly to demonstrate a baseline feasibility.

propositional logic

As mentioned in the page introduction, a primary goal of propositional logic is to expose the student to formal science in general and Boolean logic in particular on familiar ground.

A rather stilted teacher/classroom interaction is used to introduce the teacher to a perspective of propositional logic, excuse me, a perspective of the formalization of propositional logic appropriate for this level of education: as a game that only cares about being right.

The pedagogic key to presentation is the truth table demo, which gives immediate visual confirmation of an expression's value for any given input.

Good morning children. I am Jack, and here to talk to you about something really amazing: logic.

[In the sea of faces we see the curious, the skeptical, some signs of groans. We press on.]

Any questions?

[A hand  shoots up. A mischievous face.]

Yes?

[ "Is logic logical?" Giggles heard.]

An interesting question, um ...

["Jill."]

Well, Jill, you just used a clever bit of logic, and I stand corrected. I'm not going to talk about logic. I'm going to talk about a formal logic; specifically, I am going to talk about propositional logic. And a formal logic, like propositional logic, cares more about being right than being logical; it just doesn't want to be wrong. That's why its always supposing. And it supposes a lot of things.

And it begins by supposing a proposition is a statement that can be judged to be true or false.

["Aren't all statements either true or false?"]

Well Jill, I don't know, but I think maybe not. There are formal logics where you do not suppose all statements are either true or false, since some logicians think this may be relevant in some cases; but whatever is 'logically correct', propositional logic supposes that a proposition can always be judged as either true or false. There is no middle ground.

In many ways, a formal logic is like a game logicians invent to imitate a small slice of what we might call logical decision making. So if you play the games by the rules, and the game imitates logical thinking, you're thinking logically when you play the game, since you can't be wrong.

But to always be right, you have to suppose a lot of things, and you have to not care about a lot of things. For example here are two statements.
  • It is raining.
  • It is dark.

We assume circumstances are such that each question

  • Is it raining?
  • Is it dark?

can be answered with a yes or no. That is, we assume the two statements are propositions. But the game doesn't really care if it is raining or if it is dark; it only cares the proposition has been assigned a truth value: it supposes these  propositions have been assigned these truth values; it does not suppose the truth values assigned are accurate. This is not a judgment propositional logic makes, since it could be wrong.

Propositional logic provides rules for combining propositions and constructing propositional expressions.

Its a pain to write out the full statement every time you want to refer to a proposition, especially since the only thing you care about is whether it is true or false. So we name propositions, in order to refer to them more easily. For example, we might use names like

  •  'It is raining" is named ℛℛ 
  • "It is dark" is  named 𝒟𝒟
The names don't matter much. Short is good. In fact, we are not in first grade anymore. We can think of any four propositions we want; but so we are all on the same page, we will all name the four propositions we are thinking about as pp, qq, rr and ss. On this page, these names are rather magical. When you use them to construct propositional expressions, and color them rusty red, when you click on them, it brings you to the truth table for the propositional expression.

The truth table for 𝑝 (or 𝑟) shows that a proposition is a propositional expression, but a very boring one. The value of the propositional expression is the value of the proposition.

A slightly less boring propositional expression can be constructed by using the not operator, Like all operators, the not operator will be assigned a symbol; the not operator is denoted by the ¬\not symbol. The not operator reverses a proposition's truth value, e.g. consider the expressions ¬ 𝑝 or ¬ 𝑟, etc.

The not operator is a bit of an exception. It constructs a propositional expression from a single proposition. All other operators construct a propositional expression from two propositions.

The propositional expression constructed from the and operator, denoted by the ∧∧ symbol, is true if both propositions are true, and false if either proposition is false. For example consider the propositional expressions 𝑝 ∧ 𝑞 or 𝑞 ∧ 𝑠, etc.

The propositional expression constructed from the or operator, denoted by the ∨∨ symbol, is true if either propositions is true, and false if both propositions are false. For example consider the propositional expressions 𝑝 ∨ 𝑞 or 𝑞 ∨ 𝑠, etc.

The propositional expression constructed from the same operator, denoted by the ↔↔ symbol, is true if both propositions have the same truth value, and is false if the propositions have different truth values. For example consider the propositional expressions 𝑝  ↔  𝑞 or 𝑞  ↔  𝑠, etc.

Here's a table listing the symbol names of these basic operators.
 logical operation
 symbol naming it
 not
       ¬\not
 and
       ∧∧
 or
       ∨∨
 same
      ↔↔

The not operator can not only negate (i.e. reverse) a proposition, it can reverse a propositional expression. Consider some examples
  • ¬ [ 𝑝 ∧ 𝑞 ] 
  • ¬ [ 𝑝 ∨ 𝑞 ] 
  • ¬ [ 𝑝  ↔  𝑞 ] 
  • ¬ [ ¬ 𝑝 ] 

The other operators can not only combine two proposition, they can combine two propositional expressions, for example

  • 𝑝 ∧ [ 𝑞 ∨ 𝑟 ] 
  • [ 𝑝 ∧ 𝑞 ] ∨ 𝑟 
  • ¬ 𝑝 ∨ 𝑞 
  • ¬ [ ¬ 𝑝 ]  ↔  𝑝
The last propositional expression listed is what is called a tautology. Now that's a word that might impress your parents. When they ask you what you learned about in school, when you casually say, 'not much, just about, you know, logical tautologies', they may be so impressed or flummoxed they might forget to ask you if you did your homework.

[a few laughs]

And now you know a tautology is just a fancy word for a propositional expression that is always true, no matter the truth value of any proposition in the expression.

The third propositional expression listed, ¬p∨q\notp∨q, is used so often it is written as p→qp\toq. The truth table recognizes this definition, and so
  • [ ¬ 𝑝 ∨ 𝑞 ]  ↔  [ 𝑝 → 𝑞 ] 
is a tautology. This operation is called implication, and is denoted by the →\to symbol. We note
  • [ [ 𝑝 → 𝑞 ] ∧ [ 𝑞 → 𝑝 ] ]  ↔  [ 𝑝  ↔  𝑞 ] 

is a tautology.

Tautologies can be use to prove so called properties of logical operations. For example, the and operation ∧∧, the or operation ∨∨, and the same operation ↔↔ are commutative. This means the order of the two propositions does not matter, as the following tautologies show:

  • [ 𝑝 ∧ 𝑞 ]  ↔  [ 𝑞 ∧ 𝑝 ]
  • [ 𝑝 ∨ 𝑞 ]  ↔  [ 𝑞 ∨ 𝑝 ]   
  • [ 𝑝  ↔  𝑞 ]  ↔  [ 𝑞  ↔  𝑝 ] 
Tautologies also show these three operations are also associative, as shown by:
  • [ [ 𝑝 ∧ 𝑞 ] ∧ 𝑟 ]  ↔  [ 𝑝 ∧ [ 𝑞 ∧ 𝑟 ] ] 
  • [ [ 𝑝 ∨ 𝑞 ] ∨ 𝑟 ]  ↔  [ 𝑝 ∨ [ 𝑞 ∨ 𝑟 ] ] 
  • [ [ 𝑝  ↔  𝑞 ]  ↔  𝑟 ]  ↔  [ 𝑝  ↔  [ 𝑞  ↔  𝑟 ] ] 

Well this is all okay, but what is it good for you might ask.

["Yes we might." Some smiles.]

Well for one thing you just learned Boolean logic. Slip that into your dinner conversation and your parents won't dare ask about homework for a week.

[lighter laughs; jokes get old.]

Of course, you're not experts yet. Some experts use Boolean logic to find the truth values of propositional expressions constructed from millions of propositions. We'd need a pretty big truth table to handle that.

But we are learning propositional logic for a very specific reason: a propositional expression provides the skeletal structure of a formal statement, and formal statements are important in science.

formal statements


The subject of formal statements naturally follows the subject of propositional logic. This is because quantified predicates are propositions, and a quantified predicate expression is a propositional expression.

We want to make statements about collections. As our target is basic education, we can comfortably limit ourselves to collections of cardinality easily handled by standard set theory. We adopt the perspective established by axiomatized ZF set theory. As the only type is set, we can use the language of classical single-sorted first order predicate logic.

We assume a universal collection of sets, and denote it with 𝒱𝒱. This collection, on pain of paradox, cannot be a set. But we use it to describe the universal predicate of our adopted set theory: membership, which we denote
  • ∊:𝒱×𝒱→𝔹\in:𝒱\times𝒱\to𝔹  
where 𝔹𝔹 is a binary set whose members are interpreted as Boolean truth values; this is analogous to how standard predicates will be handled. Unlike standard predicates, like (propositional) logical operators, the membership predicate is part of our formal language based on vanilla FOL.

We do not discuss the topic of inference mechanisms; we are only interested in the language, and specifically, simple quantified predicate expressions. The goal is not mastery of the language of FOL It is a concrete means of allowing the student to become familiar with the notion of a formal statement.

set constructors

We assume two basic set constructors
  • product, denoted ×\times
  • and directed pair, denoted →\to 
A product combines sets where, besides bookkeeping, the order of factors is insignificant. The order of sets in a directed pair is relevant. There is a from or domain set, and a to or codomain set. At this basic level, we prohibit (even thinking about) a directed pair from being used as a domain or codomain of any directed pair.

function

A function is
  • a directed pair
  • and a rule that assigns to any member of the domain, a member of the codomain.

For example - given addition is defined for the naturals -

  • ℕ→ℕℕ\toℕ
  • add 2 to any member of the domain

and

  • ℕ×ℕ→ℕℕ\timesℕ\toℕ
  • add the product factors

are functions. A function is often identified by prepending the directed pair with a name [colon]; e.g.

  • add_two: ℕ→ℕℕ\toℕ
might refer to the function that adds 2 to the input.

predicate

A predicate is a function whose codomain is the binary set of Boolean truth values. Thus if 𝒮𝒮 is any set, any function defined for the directed pair
  • 𝒮→𝔹𝒮\to𝔹
is a predicate. For example, if
  • P:ℕ×ℕ→𝔹,(where𝒮≡ℕ×ℕ)P: ℕ\timesℕ\to𝔹,\mathrm{\;(where\;}𝒮\equivℕ\timesℕ)
  • andletting(x1,x2)∊ℕ×ℕ,(x1,x2)↦{trueifx1<x2falseif¬(x1<x2)\mathrm{and\;letting\;}(x_1,x_2)\inℕ\timesℕ,\;(x_1,x_2)↦\begin{cases} \mathrm{true\;if\;}x_1<x_2 \\ \mathrm{false\;if\;}\not(x_1<x_2) \end{cases} 
then PP is a predicate.

predicate expression

The same set of logical operators developed for constructing propositional expressions can be used to construct predicate expressions.

quantification

A predicate expression may be quantified.

The goal is to expose the student to experience with simple quantified expressions.

Well hello all, look whose back, its Jack.

[Grunts.]

Hey, its OK; its your secret if you can't stop thinking about propositions.

[Grimaces and grunts.]

OK; propositions are kind of boring. But don't worry. I am here to vanquish them to a small role on a much larger stage, but first (ahem) I must set the stage.

[Eye-rolling groans.]

We all know what a collection is right; and many might have heard of set theory. Did you know not all collections are sets; some are too big. Sets can be really, really big, so this will not be a problem for us, and we can safely think of a set as a collection.

["But how can a collection be too big to be a set?" Inquisitive faces.]

Hello Jill, nice to see you. Well, a set is a mathematical term, a very important mathematical term. A set not only has a mathematical definition, it has a whole theory devoted to it. But as it turns out, not all collections are sets. Some are just too big to fit inside the precise mathematical definition. For example the collection of all sets is not a set. If you try to treat this collection as a set, paradoxes arise: you can draw contradicting conclusions; all very confusing. And I'm no expert Jill. Sometimes, at least until we have learned so for ourselves, we just have to trust established mathematical fact as fact.

["OK, so you just warned us about something we don't have to worry about?" Sounds of amused agreement.]

Ha ha, I guess so Jill. But it does suggest a set is more than a collection. There are rules that define limits, even if for us those limits are far, far away and collections will always be sets. And per the jargon of some logicians, set will be a primitive notion, meaning we won't try to formally define or describe it: its our intuition of a collection.

But we will formally describe two set constructors, namely the
  • product
  • and directed-pair
constructors which construct sets from sets. So we will need some base sets for out constructors. A good example of a base set is the set of natural numbers. Another example is the binary set of Boolean truth values. Remember those, the possible values of a proposition?

A product is a set whose members are tuples. A tuple is a sequence of slots, but aside from identification, the order of slots doesn't matter. Each slot is bound to a set. The value of the slot will always be a member of the (bound) set. Multiple slots in a tuple may be bound to the same or different sets.

More specifically, the product is the set of all possible such (bound) tuples.

A product is denoted by the sets to which the tuple slots are bound. The times symbol is used to separate the sets. For instance
  • if members of the product are tuples with two slots, each of which is bound to the natural numbers (denoted ℕℕ) then
    • the product would be denoted by ℕ×ℕℕ\timesℕ.
["OK, but what has this to do with a product?"]

You mean multiplication, like in arithmetic?

["yes."]

Not much Jill. Worse, sometimes the sets are referred to as product factors. Maybe sometimes we just run out of words and reuse them? I don't know. But at least we now know what they're talking about right?

[Murmured denials.]

But the product is used to help describe arithmetic. First though, we describe a directed-pair.

A directed-pair is constructed from two sets; one is called the domain, the other the codomain.

We use a directed-pair when we want to formally define a function. A function is
  • a directed-pair
  • and a rule that can assign to any member of the domain a member of the codomain.

Using an arrow to separate the domain and codomain, both addition and multiplication of natural numbers can be described as

  • the directed pair: ℕ×ℕ→ℕℕ\timesℕ\toℕ
  • and a rule for adding or multiplying tuple values.

Any questions?

["Can a directed-pair be a domain or codomain?"]

Ah, good question. Perhaps so. Sounds like a good start for describing a function between functions. But for now, let's say we won't use directed-pairs for domains or codomains. I think that's a good idea; keep things simple.

[Mostly puzzled acknowledgment.]

Anyway, a set constructor product has nothing to do with multiplication. Its just a set constructor name.

OK. We have our primitive notion of a set and two example sets:

  • the natural numbers ℕ≡{1,2,⋯}ℕ\equiv\{1,2,⋯\} 
  • and the set of Boolean truth values 𝔹≡{true,false}𝔹\equiv\{true,false\}.

We have described two set constructors: product and directed-pair.

We have a formal definition of function. When describing a function, we will often use the following convention:

  • we provide a name or symbol identifier for the function followed, by a colon and the directed-pair, and
  • considering a base set as a tuple with a single slot,
    • we provide a domain tuple with each slot labeled by a variable,
    • and a description of how these variables determine the codomain member
    • where the tuple and description are separated by the ↦↦ symbol.

For example, consider the addition of two natural numbers. Then we would have

  • ∀x₁ ∃x₂ [ PG(x₁,x₂) ] 

We are in a good position to define the core component of formal statements - are you ready? - ta da: the predicate.

A predicate is a function whose (directed-pair's) codomain is the set of Boolean truth values 𝔹𝔹.

If you feel a bit let down after all that fanfare, good. A predicate is that simple.

A simple example is the greater than predicate that compares two natural numbers. We can give this predicate a formal definition:

  • ∀x₁ ∃x₂ [ PG(x₁,x₂) ]

We can consider an even simpler predicate. We can consider whether a natural number is less than 10. Can you guess what it's formal definition might look like? Its one of those cases where we should consider a base set as a single-slot tuple. We give a definition.

  • ∀x₁ ∃x₂ [ PG(x₁,x₂) ]
A predicate is neither true nor false; but we may ask if there is some natural number greater than 10, or whether all natural numbers are greater than 10, where clearly, the first question should  be answered yes and the second no. They are propositions. A predicate can be turned into a proposition, you remember, a statement which is always either true or false.

There is a fancy word when checking whether a predicate is true for some domain member or all domain members: quantification. Logicians seen to be a rather formal bunch; their language seems a bit stilted, but they mean well, so we live it, right guys?

[Blank stares.]

Anyway, they refer to quantifiers:
  • there exists, denoted ∃∃, when asking if there is some domain member associated with the true codomain member, and
  • for all, denoted ∀∀, when asking if all domain members are associated with the true codomain member.

Does everyone see a quantified predicate is a proposition? It will always be either true or false.

In the simplest case of a single-slot predicate, such as the greater than 10 predicate formalized above, quantification is pretty simple. We either have

  • ∃x[P(x)]∃x[P(x)] or ∀x[P(x)]∀x[P(x)], where P≡greaterthan10P\equiv\mathrm{greater\;than\;10}
both of which are straightforward to interpret, i.e. the first is a true proposition, and the second is false. Easy enough to see, I think. Everyone agree?

["What's that x?"]

That is a great question. You see, you don't quantify a predicate directly; you don't even quantify a tuple slot. Rather, you quantify a variable bound to the slot. This variable may be any member of the set to which the slot is bound.

In fact, what we really want to quantify is a predicate expression. If we quantify all the predicates in a predicate expression, we would be dealing with a propositional expression, the same propositional expressions we talked about when you were only children, but you might remember some things about them.

But considering a predicate expression complicates things a bit. For example
  • let P1≡greaterthan10P_1\equivgreater\;than\;10 and P2≡lessthan20P_2\equivless\;than\;20
  • and consider the quantified predicate expressions
    •  ∃x,y[P1(x)∧P2(y)]∃x,y[P_1(x)∧P_2(y)] and ∃x[P1(x)∧P2(x)]∃x[P_1(x)∧P_2(x)].
Can you see that the first one will always be true, while the second will always be false because of the way we bind variables to slots? In th first expression, each predicate has it's own variable. It is easy to find two numbers that will satisfy the expression. On the other hand, how is one number going to satisfy both predicates?

Do you remember what a tautology is? This may help. Let P≡greaterthan10P\equivgreater\;than\;10. Then
  • ∀x[P(x)∨¬P(x)]∀x[P(x)∨\notP(x)].
When a predicate, such as the greaterthangreater\;than predicate, has more than one slot, things become a bit more complicated, because we might now have to consider the order of mixed quantifiers. For example
  • let P≡greaterthanP\equivgreater\;than, and consider the quantified predicate expressions
    • ∀x ∃y [ 𝑃(x,y) ] and ∃y ∀x [ 𝑃(x,y)≀].
These are different propositions. The first is true. The second is false. Some people see this easily. Some don't. I don't; I have to think about it, and eventually I can say, oh sure, like it was always easy to see.

It would be nice to have something like the truth table demo that we used to visualize propositional expressions that we could use to help visualize quantified predicate expressions, wouldn't it? We can't use a truth table because there are way too many possible combinations to enumerate. In addition, the visualization tool needs to understand the predicate rule in order to evaluate all possible predicate values.

So we have to keep things simple. The visualization tool is called the formal statement demo. Its pretty simple, but sometimes simple helps.

There are only four builtin predicates
  • PG5≡greaterthan5PG5\equivgreater\;than\;5 
  • PL10≡lessthan10PL10\equivless\;than10
  • PG≡greaterthanPG\equivgreater\;than 
  • PL≡lessthanPL\equivless\;than
where the first two predicates are single-slotted, and the last two predicates listed have two slots. Formally, we have four predicates
  • ∀x₁ ∃x₂ [ PG(x₁,x₂) ] 
  • ∀x₁ ∃x₂ [ PG(x₁,x₂) ]
  • ∀x₁ ∃x₂ [ PG(x₁,x₂) ]
  • ∀x₁ ∃x₂ [ PG(x₁,x₂) ]

that the user can choose from to make a valid predicate expression. At this point, there is no difference between a valid predicate expression and a valid propositional expression, and the predicate names can be used as if they label propositions. You are able to construct predicate expressions in the same way you constructed propositional expressions in the truth table demo.

But after you've constructed a valid predicate expression, you must bind each slot in each predicate to a variable. In extreme cases, you may assign the same variable to every slot, or a different variable to each slot, or any combination you choose.

Then, you choose a sequence of quantifiers that bind all the variables.

The demo should now be able to determine the truth value of the quantified predicate expression, and provide visual aids to explain why it has this value. This should help those like me who need some time and examples before we can understand a quantified predicate. Its not always obvious.

numbers

By the time the subject of a formal description of numbers is presented to students, they should already be well versed in basic number literacy. The formal description will not facilitate calculation. Rather the goal is provide a formal foundation for a formal means of describing the validity of a mathematical model that bypasses the set's intrinsic spaces of continuity and measure, determined by constrained choices (referred to as a topology and a σσ-algebra) of a member of the set's powerset, the support standard analysis and measure theory. In addition, no algebraic structure is required, or possible really.

Of course, we are describing core topics. Intrinsic spaces and algebraic structures are essential for the STEM-oriented student.

We can, from our tertiary level of understanding, describe three sets of numbers defined by transfinite inductive definitions, and whose birthday is less than or equal to ωω (omega), the first non-finite ordinal. All three sets have a single root member. Their difference is determined by the number of successor functions in the definition, which is 1, 2, or 4.

When the number of successor functions is 1, only one additional member is added to the set of natural numbers, namely ωω. Defining the set
  • ℕω≡ℕ⋃{ω}ℕ_ω\equivℕ⋃\{ω\} 

isn't very interesting. But it does introduce the critical notion of introducing ωω as a member, like any other, of a set of numbers like .e.g. ℕωℕ_ω.

Things get interesting when the number of successors is 2 or 4, and the (inclusive) induction cutoff is ωω. Here, we define sets

  • ℝω≡{thedyadicrationals}⋃{(2successor)numberswhosebirthdayisω}ℝ_ω\equiv \{\mathrm{the\;dyadic\;rationals}\}⋃ \{\mathrm{(2\;successor)\;numbers\;whose\;birthday\;is\;ω}\}
  • ℂω≡{dyadiccomplexnumbers}⋃{(4successor)numberswhosebirthdayisω}ℂ_ω\equiv \{\mathrm{dyadic\;complex\;numbers}\}⋃ \{\mathrm{(4\;successor)\;numbers\;whose\;birthday\;is\;ω}\}  

and where ℝ⊂ℝωℝ⊂ℝ_ω and ℂ⊂ℂωℂ⊂ℂ_ω.

Without further reflection, we might think we'd leave ℝωℝ_ω and ℂωℂ_ω for STEM-oriented students, and extract ℝℝ and ℂℂ for our core number sets, but we adopt the opposite approach: ℝωℝ_ω and ℂωℂ_ω are the core number sets, and ℝℝ and ℂℂ are extracted for STEM-oriented topics such as intrinsic spaces and algebraic structure. This choice provides a framework for nonstandard analysis and measure, as we now have simple transfinite transect and grid at our disposal.

Of course, we are discussing things top down. We certainly don't want to include transfinite induction as part of the origin narrative. We haven't even formally defined union. But we note an important pattern shared by ℝwℝ_w and ℂωℂ_ω that facilitates a simpler description

  • there is a countable set generated by finite induction
  • there is an uncountable set generated by induction whose birthday is ωω 
  • and the countable set is dense in their union.

We can use the recursive definitions of order and field level arithmetic pioneered by John Conway to define operations that work for finite induction and extend to work for induction step ωω.
